THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, TUESDAY, OCTOBER 3, 1933

THE BOOK PAGE

SOVIET STATISTICS

SUMMARY OF THE FULFILMENT OF THE
FIRST FIVE-YEAR PLAN FOR THE
DEVELOPMENT OF THE NATIONAL
ECONOMY OF THE U.S.S.R. Report
of the State Planning Commission
of the Council of People's Commis-
sars of the Union of Soviet Social-
ist Republics. State Planning Com-
mission of the U.S.S.R., Moscow.
Allen & Unwin, London. Cloth 7/6.
Paper 5/-.

This review by Lord Marley will be
read with interest but it does not
express the opinions of this journal.

There is in China at the present
time considerable discussion of
what is known as "planned national
economy." The National Govern-
ment is said to be establishing a
National Economy Council at Nan-
king, whose task will be to study
the economic position of China, and
the best means of increasing indus-
trial and agricultural production.
Somewhat similar conditions exist-
ed in Russia immediately after the
war, and a study of the methods
employed and the successes achiev-
ed in that country might well be of
decisive importance in China. For
this reason the appearance of the
U.S.S.R. official account of the
fulfilment of the First Five-Year
Plan is of very great interest.
The volume is rightly termed a
"summary," but contains a wealth
of information upon so many
aspects of national life in the Soviet
Union that it should prove of real
interest to a wide circle of ordinary
readers who seek information on
this thorny and much disputed
subject. For these readers let me
say that the volume under review is
well got up, excellently printed on
good paper, and written in a read-
able and not too technical manner.
There is a general summary of the
"planned guidance of the whole
economy of the country," due to the
concentration of the key economic
positions in the hands of the State,
"as compared with the character-
istic features of capitalism, anarchy
and competition, which have become
particularly acute in the period of
Imperialism." This summary is
followed by chapters on industry,
agriculture, transport, living condi-
tions, finance, and education. Final-
ly there is a most interesting
study of the method of division of
labour applied to a vast area such
as the Soviet Union. The aim is to
secure that factories are placed
near to sources of raw materials,
and related to the supply of power,
the whole problem being studied
with a view to meet the needs of
the vast population in the cheapest
and most efficient manner.

There is, of course, much
statistical matter in this account of
progress, and it is often suggested
that Russian Government statistics
are inaccurate, or are deliberately
falsified so as to give a more
favourable picture than the facts
justify. It is said that statistics
can be made to prove anything.
Certainly no statistics are complete-
ly accurate, and in a country so
vast and undeveloped as the
U.S.S.R. it would be rash to claim
that there are no errors. Never-
theless it is worth recording that
Tsarist Russia led the world in
statistical theory. Since the present
regime this theory has been
developed, improved and for the
first time made full use of on the
actual basis upon which the whole
economic planning of the U.S.S.R.
is built up. In consequence the
accuracy of statistics has become of
far greater importance in Russia
than in any other country; it can
hardly be asserted that the Govern-
ment would have two different sets
of statistics, one for home use and
one to delude the foreigner.
Probably, taking into account the
extent of the Soviet Union and the
difficulties of communication, soviet
statistics may be considered re-
markably reliable. The present
writer had an opportunity of
examining the returns upon which
these statistics are built up, and
after a full discussion with (Prince)
Obolensky Ossinsky, head of the
Government statistical department,
he does not consider that the
figures can reasonably be assailed.

The basic intention of the Five-
Year Plan was to build up an
industry capable of supplying
consumption goods, so as to raise
the whole standard of life of the
workers and peasants. It meant
the sacrifice of certain comforts
for a few years in order that ex-
ports might be increased to pay for
imports of machinery to equip the
production factories. Much else
was of course included, and the
whole story of this development is
fascinating, including as it does a
frank description of the failures as
well as the successes. For example,
the lag in the increase of produc-
tivity of labour is admitted and
explained. The huge task set to
the railways, not only in building
new lines (the mileage increased
from 58,000 kilometres in 1913 to
83,000 kilometres in 1932), but in
strengthening the roads and bridges,
doubling and trebling tracks, instal-
ling block signalling and building
new locomotives and rolling stock,
is described in one of the most
interesting chapters. Newspaper
men will read with envy of the
increase in circulation of soviet
newspapers, from 8 million copies
in 1928 to 35 million copies in
1932. Russian newspapers are now
published in eighty-eight langu-
ages. Coal is among those produc-
tive industries which failed to
reach the planned figures. Electri-
fication far surpassed the plan, and
it is not infrequent, even in remote
parts of the Union, to find electric
power for irrigation and electric
light in villages far distant from
any railway but served by over-
head cable lines.

The general reader will, however,
turn first to an account of living
conditions in Russia, and the
chapter headed "Labour and Living
Conditions," when studied in con-
junction with the tables at the end
of the volume, together give a fair
idea of the position, particularly
in comparison with Great Britain,
Germany, and the United States.
The population of the U.S.S.R. was
154 million in 1929, and is increas-
ing at a rate of over three million
a year. This year it is 166 million.
During the same period the number
of workers has more than doubled
(from 11 million to 23 million) and
unemployment has been entirely
eliminated. There is an interesting
account of the means by which the
worker acquires a new attitude to
labour, regarding it as a matter of
honour by his example to educate
and awaken the enthusiasm of other
more backward workers. The

《字林西报》，1933年10月3日，星期二

书评版

苏联统计资料

《苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟国民经济发展第一个五年计划执行情况摘要》。苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟人民委员会国家计划委员会报告。苏联国家计划委员会，莫斯科。艾伦与昂温出版社（Allen & Unwin），伦敦。布面精装7先令6便士。平装5先令。

马利勋爵（Lord Marley）的这篇评论读来饶有趣味，但并不代表本刊观点。

目前，中国国内对于所谓“计划国民经济”有着广泛的讨论。据悉，国民政府正在南京设立一个国民经济委员会，其任务是研究中国的经济状况，以及增加工农业生产的最有效手段。俄国在战后不久也存在着类似的情况，因此研究该国所采用的方法及其取得的成就，对中国而言可能具有决定性的重要意义。出于这个原因，苏联官方发布的关于第一个五年计划执行情况的报告引起了极大的关注。

该书恰如其分地被称为“摘要”，但其中包含了有关苏联国民生活诸多方面的丰富信息，对于那些寻求了解这一棘手且争议颇多之主题的广大普通读者来说，它确实具有真正的吸引力。对于这些读者，我要说的是，这本受评之书装帧精良，纸质优良，印刷精美，行文通俗易懂，不过于技术化。书中首先对“全国经济的计划指导”进行了总体概述，这归功于将关键经济命脉集中在国家手中，“这与资本主义的特征——无政府状态和竞争——形成对比，而这些特征在帝国主义时期变得尤为尖锐。”在这一概述之后，是有关工业、农业、交通、生活条件、财政和教育的章节。最后，还有一项极为有趣的研究，探讨了在苏联这样广袤的地区所应用的劳动分工方法。其目的是确保工厂靠近原材料产地，并与电力供应相协调，研究整个问题的出发点是以最廉价、最高效的方式满足庞大人口的需求。

当然，这份关于进步的报告中包含大量的统计数据，人们经常指出，俄罗斯政府的统计数据不准确，或者是故意伪造，以呈现出比事实更为有利的图景。有人说，统计数据可以被用来证明任何事情。诚然，没有任何统计数据是完全准确的，而在像苏联这样幅员辽阔且不发达的国家，声称没有任何错误将是轻率的。然而，值得记录的是，沙皇俄国在统计理论方面曾领先世界。自现政权建立以来，这一理论得到了发展和改进，并首次在构建苏联整体经济规划的实际基础上得到了充分利用。因此，统计数据的准确性在俄罗斯变得比在任何其他国家都重要得多；很难断言政府会拥有两套不同的统计数据，一套供国内使用，另一套用于欺骗外国人。考虑到苏联的幅员辽阔和通讯困难，苏联的统计数据或许可以被认为是相当可靠的。笔者有机会审查了构成这些统计数据基础的报表，并在与政府统计部门负责人奥博连斯基-奥辛斯基亲王（(Prince) Obolensky Ossinsky）进行充分讨论后，认为这些数据难以受到合理的质疑。

五年计划的基本意图是建立一个能够供应消费品的工业体系，从而提高工人和农民的整体生活水平。这意味着在几年内牺牲某些舒适享受，以便增加出口，从而支付进口生产工厂所需机械的费用。当然，计划还包括许多其他内容，这一发展的整个过程引人入胜，其中包括坦率地描述了失败以及成功。例如，书中承认并解释了劳动生产率增长的滞后。铁路面临的巨大任务在其中一个最有趣的章节中得到了描述，这不仅包括建设新线路（里程从1913年的58,000公里增加到1932年的83,000公里），还包括加固道路和桥梁，将轨道加倍甚至三倍，安装闭塞信号系统，以及制造新的机车和车辆。报业人士读到苏联报纸发行量的增长时定会心生羡慕，从1928年的800万份增加到1932年的3500万份。俄罗斯报纸现在以八十八种语言出版。煤炭是未能达到计划产量的生产行业之一。电气化程度远远超过了计划，即使在联盟的偏远地区，也经常可以看到用于灌溉的电力和电灯，这些村庄远离任何铁路，但由架空电缆线路供电。

然而，普通读者首先会转向关于俄罗斯生活状况的描述，题为“劳动与生活条件”的章节，结合卷末的表格一起研读，可以让人对当时的状况有一个公正的了解，特别是与英国、德国和美国相比。1929年苏联人口为1.54亿，并以每年超过300万的速度增长。今年人口为1.66亿。在同一时期，工人数量增加了一倍多（从1100万增加到2300万），失业现象已完全消除。书中有趣地描述了工人如何获得新的劳动态度，将其视为一种荣誉，并通过自己的榜样来教育和唤醒其他较为落后的工人的热情。该

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, TUESDAY, OCTOBER 3, 1933

IMPARTIAL NOT NEUTRAL

IN RUSSIA NOW

The Soviet balloon, U.S.S.R., has deftly put on record a fine feat which should supplement Professor August Picard's work in adding to the world's knowledge of happenings on the other side of the airman's ceiling. Roughly stated, the Russian scientists reached a height three times that of Mount Everest. The physical endurance during the comparatively short ascent was great. Amazingly it is recorded that, inside the car of the balloon, one of the discomforts was heat —the temperature being actually 98 degrees higher than the readings outside. The Soviet Government is to be congratulated on this notable feat which, naturally, formed the theme of enthusiastic political speeches by exulting Commissars when the balloon returned to earth. It is to be hoped that the success, linked with a more normal international relationship, will tend to eliminate the aggressively propagandist apologies which Russian spokesmen and their sympathisers seem to find necessary in order to rid themselves of a feeling of inferiority when in contact with other systems of administration. Correspondence in these columns has lately shown a marked divergence of view regarding the conditions in Russia and, especially, the working of the Five Year Plan. On the book page to-day Lord Marley reviews the recently issued official report of the Soviet Government on that plan. It has been made available by the enterprise of Messrs. Allen and Unwin, the London publishers, whose attention to documentary evidence of modern international thought has been so marked a feature of their publishing policy. Discrepancy of information on Russia is bound to prevail, so long as the country is so much a closed book. Moreover, the very magnitude of the territory covered by the U.S.S.R. makes it probable that material proof can always be found to support any particular theory.

Naturally the official summary endeavours to make the Five Year Plan appear as successful as possible. Lord Marley seems to give the document most respectful consideration—as is fit and proper—but also too easy-going an acceptance of its figures, as will be shown in due course. The trial of the British engineers, the information derived with no special propaganda intent and other factors suggest that the figures as well as the rosy deductions concerning the

Plan should be accepted with considerable reserve. With the form of administration set up to guide the Russian people through a period of reconstruction outsiders have no desire to concern themselves, so long as there is no attempt to claim for that system the right of general application in the world at large. A Government, manned in large measure by men untrained in the direction of mighty events, deprived of highly-trained and scientific assistance, mainly by its own peculiar decision to elevate the "proletariat," and working by means of an unashamed tyranny, using the fearsome instruments of murder and terrorism, had to learn by the accumulation of colossal error. The error is still there and the Government is still, presumably learning, although he would be a bold man who would venture exactly to define the stability of the administration in power. The Five Year Plan has been kept on the rails only by the exercise of the fiercest pressure on the Russian people. It is not too much to say that the destitution, starvation and misery through which the Russian masses are likely to go during the present winter exceed anything in other distressed regions of a distressed world. In fairness it must be recognised that, in spite of their reliance on barbarous methods, the Soviet authorities have been able to inspire a strong missionary zeal which plainly keeps the general morale from collapsing. Hence come, perhaps, the directly contradictory pictures drawn by correspondents who have been contributing to these columns.

The chief charge to be made against Moscow by other nations is this: never in modern history have the nations, nominally at peace, had to incur such heavy expenditure in policing themselves against the activities of propagandist agents of a single country as have the chief Powers of the world been forced to do in face of the operations of the Comintern. Devastation and bloodshed in China tell that tale grimly. The task of assessing Russian achievements is enormously hampered by the fear that occupation in it may, in some way or other, assist that network of world-conspiracy. The violence of the counter-propaganda defeated itself. Intellectuals, out of a sense of proportion slightly awry, rebelled. They refused to recognise the plain facts of the paucity of technical skill and real intellect, as distinct from genius, in Russia as a whole. They delivered themselves up to "personally-conducted tours" in Moscow. Their intentions were admirable. The results were unfortunate. There came to be a deep gulf between those who went to Russia prepared to admire and those who professed to "see things as they were" but were just as biassed in the other direction. The truth, as usual, seems to lie between the two extremes. That is where Lord Marley elects to go astray. It would be interesting to know if his school of thought would be so fertile in excuses, so decorous in language if the subject of examination were, for example, Hitlerist Germany or Fascist Italy. Yesterday the Russian method of disposing of the word "unemployment" was explained in these columns. That supplies appropriate comment on Lord Marley's comfortable assertion that there is "no unemployment" in Russia. For the rest let his handling of statistics be noted. He accepts the statements that in the five years higher education pupils have increased in number from 600,000 to 3,000,000 and elementary pupils from 11,000,-000 to 23,000,000. Any educationalist will agree that these figures are preposterous. It is not necessary to consider cost alone, but the actual machinery required to obtain those results. In England when the raising of the school age from 14 to 16 was discussed, it was revealed that to handle the 400,000 additional pupils thus involved would throw a terrific strain on the finances of the local authorities. The provision of the additional accommodation and teaching staffs would demand at least three or four years' notice. Russia is admittedly short of technical experts. Can it be conceived that in five years she could train up sufficient teachers to cope with an additional 12,000,000 elementary school-children and—more absurd still—2,400,000 higher education pupils. It is toward these and similar assertions that the reader has to show the utmost caution in examining Russian claims. Lord Marley would be more convincing if, in his otherwise illuminating review, he had displayed that acutely critical scepticism which he is so ready to apply to the institutions and loyalties of his own country.

《字林西报》，1933年10月3日，星期二

公正而非中立

当下的俄国

苏联气球“苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟号”（U.S.S.R.）巧妙地创下了一项壮举，这一成就应当为奥古斯特·皮卡德教授的工作提供补充，从而增进世界对飞行员升限以上高空现象的了解。粗略地说，俄国科学家达到的高度是珠穆朗玛峰的三倍。在相对短暂的上升过程中，身体承受的耐力考验巨大。令人惊讶的是，据记录，在气球吊舱内，不适感之一竟是炎热——温度实际上比外部读数高出98度。苏联政府值得为此项显著成就受到祝贺，当气球返回地面时，欢欣鼓舞的委员们自然将其作为热情洋溢的政治演讲的主题。人们希望，这一成功若能与国际关系的正常化相结合，将有助于消除俄国发言人及其同情者似乎认为必要的、带有侵略性的宣传式辩解，以便他们在与其他行政体系接触时摆脱自卑感。近期本报读者来信栏显示，关于俄国状况，尤其是五年计划执行情况的观点存在显著分歧。在今日的书评版上，马利勋爵（Lord Marley）评述了苏联政府最近发布的关于该计划的官方报告。这份报告由伦敦出版商艾伦与昂温公司（Messrs. Allen and Unwin）积极促成出版，该公司对现代国际思想文献证据的关注一直是其出版政策的显著特征。只要俄国仍然像一个封闭的秘密，有关俄国的信息差异就必然存在。此外，苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟领土幅员之辽阔，使得人们很可能总能找到实质证据来支持任何特定的理论。

当然，官方摘要竭力使五年计划显得尽可能成功。马利勋爵似乎对该文件给予了最尊重的考量——这是恰当且得体的——但也过于轻易地接受了其中的数据，这一点将在适当时候予以说明。英国工程师受审案、并非出于特殊宣传意图而获得的信息以及其他因素表明，对于该计划的数据以及由此得出的乐观推论，都应持相当大的保留态度。至于为指导俄国人民度过重建时期而建立的行政形式，只要不试图声称该体系拥有在世界范围内普遍适用的权利，局外人便无意干涉。一个主要由未经过驾驭重大事件训练的人员组成、主要因其自身提升“无产阶级”的独特决定而剥夺了受过高度训练和科学辅助的支持、并通过毫不掩饰的暴政手段运作、使用谋杀和恐怖主义等可怕工具的政府，不得不通过积累巨大的错误来学习。错误依然存在，政府 presumably（想必）仍在学习，尽管敢于确切界定当前执政当局稳定性的人可谓胆量过人。五年计划之所以能维持正轨，全靠对俄国人民施加最严厉的压力。不妨说，俄国大众在今年冬天可能经历的贫困、饥饿和苦难，超过了这个动荡世界中其他受灾地区的任何情况。公平地说，必须承认，尽管依赖野蛮手段，苏联当局仍能够激发一种强烈的传教士般的热情，这显然防止了整体士气的崩溃。或许正是因此，向本报投稿的通讯员们描绘出了直接矛盾的景象。

其他国家对莫斯科的主要指责在于：在现代历史上，名义上处于和平状态的国家从未像世界主要强国面对共产国际行动时那样，被迫承担如此沉重的经费，以防范单一国家的宣传特工活动。中国的破坏与流血惨痛地证明了这一点。评估俄国成就的任务受到了极大的阻碍，因为人们担心参与其中可能会以某种方式助长那个世界阴谋网络。反宣传的激烈程度反而使其自取失败。知识分子出于略微失衡的比例感进行了反抗。他们拒绝承认俄国整体上缺乏技术技能和真正才智（区别于天才）这一明显事实。他们任由自己在莫斯科参加“专人引导的参观”。他们的意图是值得赞扬的。但结果却是不幸的。那些前往俄国准备表示钦佩的人，与那些自称“如实看待事物”但在另一方向上同样抱有偏见的人之间，出现了深深的鸿沟。真相通常似乎介于两个极端之间。而这正是马利勋爵选择误入歧途的地方。如果考察的对象是希特勒治下的德国或法西斯意大利，不知他的思想流派是否还会如此善于寻找借口，措辞如此得体，这倒是很有趣。昨日，本报解释了俄国处理“失业”一词的方法。这对马利勋爵舒适地断言俄国“没有失业”提供了恰当的评论。至于其余部分，请注意他对统计数据的处理方式。他接受了这样的说法：在五年内，高等教育学生人数从60万增加到300万，初等教育学生人数从1,100万增加到2,300万。任何教育家都会同意这些数字是荒谬的。不仅需要考虑成本，还需要考虑实现这些结果所需的实际机制。在英国，当讨论将学龄从14岁提高到16岁时，结果显示，要容纳由此涉及的40万名额外学生，将给地方当局的财政带来巨大的压力。提供额外的校舍和教学人员至少需要提前三到四年通知。众所周知，俄国缺乏技术专家。能否设想在五年内，她能培养出足够的教师来应对额外增加的1,200万小学生和——更荒谬的是——240万高等教育学生？在审视俄国的主张时，读者必须对这些及类似的说法表现出极度的谨慎。如果马利勋爵在他原本富有启发性的评论中，展现出他如此乐于应用于本国制度和忠诚度的那种敏锐的批判性怀疑态度，他会更具说服力。

档案
1933年10月4日

New Series Brings Life of Socialist State Before Us

What it is Like
THE FIVE
YEAR PLAN
3 Pence each

FORGES
AHEAD
in Soviet
Union
[4d. Post Free]

TWENTY TITLES FOR 5 SHILLINGS (5/9)

1. THE SECOND FIVE YEAR PLAN, by V. M. MOLOTOV, Chairman of the Council of People's Commissars. 80 pp. Covers the first Five Year Plan, the political line of the Second Five Year Plan, social reconstruction and Bolshevik tempo, the capitalist world and the Second Five Year Plan.
2. FORWARD TO THE SECOND FIVE YEAR PLAN OF SOCIALIST CONSTRUCTION. 40 pp. Resolutions of the 17th Party Conference of the C.P.S.U., giving the concrete details of the Second Five Year Plan.
3. THE SUCCESS OF THE FIVE YEAR PLAN. V. M. MOLOTOV. 88 pp. The achievements of the social construction contrasted with capitalist world crisis; the danger of intervention and the various lies which are told about the U.S.S.R. (dumping, forced labour, etc.) exposed.
4. THE OCTOBER REVOLUTION AND THE TRIUMPH OF SOCIALISM. 31 pp. The background of struggle to the present Socialist construction.
5. THE FULFILMENT OF THE FIRST FIVE YEAR PLAN. V. M. MOLOTOV. 88 pp. The Five Year Plan in four years and how it was done—a critical and factual review.
The next few booklets show how the workers live under the Five Year Plan, told in the form of stories. They will be of great interest, especially to trade unionists employed under capitalist industry.
6. THE FIGHT FOR STEEL. MIKAILOV. 40 pp. How "disgraceful facts" which were hampering a sheet-rolling shop were overcome.
7. KOLKOZNIKI (members of a farming "collective"). 80 pp. Collective farmers on themselves, told in a series of letters.
8. ONE OF THE 25,000. A. ISBASH. 72 pp. How Gregori Indjevastkin, one of the 25,000 whom the industrial workers sent to help organise Socialist production in the village, carried out his work in an outpost of Central Asia and was murdered just as his work reached success.
9. THE RED ARMY. 40 pp. The Socialist army—the proletarian army, the striking arm of the ruling proletariat, a genuine revolutionary fighting force of workers and peasants. How it was built up, how it is composed; the Red Army fights for peace.
10. GERMAN MINERS IN THE DONBASS. 24 pp. How unemployed miners from the Ruhr helped to build Socialism in the "Amerikanda" mine.

11. SOCIALIST COMPETITION OF THE MASSES. E. MIKULINA. 64 pp. Stalin, in his preface, says: "One of the most important factors, if not the most important factor, in our Socialist construction at the present moment is the spread of Socialist competition among the millions of the working masses."
12. WHERE THE WORKERS ARE IN POWER. D. ZASLAVSKY. 56 pp. From the old Russia to the Soviet Union, what workers' rule means: "the production of the new man."
13. HOW WORKERS BECOME ENGINEERS IN THE U.S.S.R. V. DRUZHININ. 47 pp. The Stalin Works—the apprentices, planned production, etc.
14. THE TECHNOLOGICAL AND ECONOMIC PLAN. C. M. KRZHIZHANOVSKY. 32 pp. The basis of the reconstruction.
15. SCIENCE, TECHNOLOGY AND ECONOMICS UNDER CAPITALISM AND IN THE SOVIET UNION. M. RUBINSTEIN. 48 pp. Shows how the scientific development which is paralysed and aborted by monopoly capitalism is only able to reach its full development under Socialist conditions.
16. THE SOVIET PATENT LAW. 32 pp.
17. THE SOVIET LAW ON MARRIAGE. 44 pp. The actual Code showing how women really have equal rights with man and the health and interests of mother and child are safeguarded.
18. THE PROGRAMME AND RULES OF THE C.P.S.U. (Bolsheviks). 62 pp. How the leading working-class Party in the world and the nucleus of Socialist construction is organised and its aims.
19. LOOK, YOU BOOB . . .!" 14 pp. What Bernard Shaw told the Americans about Russia.
20.* NEW CONDITIONS: NEW TASKS. 21 pp. Stalin's famous "Six Points."
FREE SOVIET LABOUR VERSUS CAPITALIST FORCED LABOUR. 44 pp. The real free basis of work in the U.S.S.R. contrasted with the bitter realities of slavery in the capitalist world.
*These two go together for 3d.

Order by the numbers.
The usual trade discounts for quantities.

新系列丛书将社会主义国家的生活展现在我们面前

其面貌如何
五年计划
每册 3 便士

在苏联
奋勇前进
[邮资 4 便士，免邮费]

二十种书目售价 5 先令（5/9）

1. 《第二个五年计划》，作者：人民委员会主席 V. M. 莫洛托夫。80 页。涵盖第一个五年计划、第二个五年计划的政治路线、社会重建与布尔什维克速度、资本主义世界与第二个五年计划。
2. 《迈向社会主义建设的第二个五年计划》。40 页。联共（布）第十七次代表会议的决议，提供第二个五年计划的具体细节。
3. 《五年计划的成功》。V. M. 莫洛托夫著。88 页。社会建设的成就与资本主义世界危机形成对比；揭露干涉的危险以及关于苏联的各种谎言（倾销、强迫劳动等）。
4. 《十月革命与社会主义的胜利》。31 页。直至当前社会主义建设的斗争背景。
5. 《第一个五年计划的完成》。V. M. 莫洛托夫著。88 页。四年内完成的五年计划及其实施过程——一项批判性与事实性的回顾。
接下来的几本小册子以故事形式展示了工人在五年计划下的生活状况。它们将引起极大兴趣，尤其是对受雇于资本主义工业下的工会成员而言。
6. 《钢铁之战》。米哈伊洛夫 (Mikhailov) 著。40 页。如何克服阻碍轧钢车间工作的“不光彩事实”。
7. 《集体农庄庄员》（农业“集体”的成员）。80 页。集体农民自述，以一系列信件的形式讲述。
8. 《二万五千人之一》。A. 伊什巴什 (Ishbash) 著。72 页。格雷戈里·因杰瓦斯特金 (Gregori Indjevastkin) 是工业工人派往农村帮助组织社会主义生产的二万五千人之一，本书讲述他在中亚前哨基地开展工作，并在工作即将取得成功时被谋杀的经历。
9. 《红军》。40 页。社会主义军队——无产阶级军队，统治无产阶级的打击力量，一支真正的工农革命战斗部队。它是如何建立起来的，其组成如何；红军为和平而战。
10. 《顿巴斯地区的德国矿工》。24 页。来自鲁尔区的失业矿工如何帮助在“阿梅里坎达” (Amerikanda) 矿井建设社会主义。

11. 《群众的社会主义竞赛》。E. 米库利娜 (Mikulina) 著。64 页。斯大林在序言中说：“如果我们目前的社会主义建设中有一个最重要的因素，那就是在数百万劳动群众中开展社会主义竞赛。”
12. 《工人掌权之地》。D. 扎斯拉夫斯基 (Zaslavsky) 著。56 页。从旧俄罗斯到苏联，工人统治意味着什么：“新人的生产”。
13. 《工人如何在苏联成为工程师》。V. 德鲁日宁 (Druzhinin) 著。47 页。斯大林工厂——学徒、计划生产等。
14. 《技术与经济计划》。C. M. 克尔日扎诺夫斯基 (Krzhizhanovsky) 著。32 页。重建的基础。
15. 《资本主义下与苏联的科学、技术和经济》。M. 鲁宾斯坦 (Rubinstein) 著。48 页。展示被垄断资本主义瘫痪和扼杀的科学发展，只有在社会主义条件下才能得到充分发展。
16. 《苏联专利法》。32 页。
17. 《苏联婚姻法》。44 页。实际法典显示妇女如何真正享有与男子平等的权利，以及母亲和儿童的健康与利益如何得到保障。
18. 《联共（布）纲领与章程》。62 页。作为世界上领先的工人阶级政党和社会主义建设核心，其组织方式及目标。
19. 《瞧，你这笨蛋……！》。14 页。萧伯纳告诉美国人关于俄罗斯的事情。
20.* 《新形势：新任务》。21 页。斯大林著名的“六点”。
《自由的苏联劳动 versus 资本主义强迫劳动》。44 页。苏联工作的真正自由基础与资本主义世界中奴隶制的残酷现实形成对比。
*这两本合售 3 便士。
